config.title: OAuth2 PKCE Flow in a SPA

intro.title: OAuth2 PKCE Flow in a SPA
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a secure login feature for a Single Page Application (SPA) using the OAuth2 Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) flow. You will learn how to generate a secret code verifier, create a challenge from it, and securely exchange an authorization code for an access token. The main technologies you'll use are React with TypeScript for the frontend and the `crypto-js` library for cryptographic operations. By the end, you'll understand how to protect your application from authorization code interception attacks while implementing a real-world authentication pattern.
intro.usecase: The OAuth2 PKCE flow is essential for securing single-page applications that integrate with third-party services like Google, GitHub, or Microsoft. Developers implement this pattern when building dashboards that display data from external APIs, such as analytics platforms showing Google Drive file statistics or project management tools syncing with GitHub repositories. This flow appears in login screens where users authenticate via "Sign in with Google" buttons, ensuring tokens are exchanged securely without exposing secrets. Every modern SPA that accesses protected resources from OAuth2 providers—from fitness apps pulling Strava data to financial dashboards connecting to banking APIs—relies on PKCE to prevent authorization code interception attacks.

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the structure of OAuth2 configuration parameters.
Implement cryptographic functions to generate a secure random code verifier using the Web Crypto API.
Utilize base64 encoding to transform the code verifier into a code challenge according to PKCE specifications.
Construct URL parameters to build the authorization endpoint URL with required OAuth2 PKCE parameters.
Control browser navigation to redirect users to the authorization server using the constructed URL.
Handle URL parsing to extract authorization code and state parameters from the callback redirect.
Execute HTTP POST requests to exchange the authorization code for an access token at the token endpoint.
Store authentication tokens securely using browser storage mechanisms with proper error handling.
Define React state hooks to manage authentication status and user information throughout the application.
Implement conditional rendering to display different UI components based on authentication state.
Invoke token validation functions to check token expiration and initiate refresh flows when needed.
Apply error handling patterns to manage OAuth2 flow failures and provide user feedback.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the React library and useState hook available for building your component.
successCriteria: The import statement should import React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you the foundation to build React components with state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using the import statement.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now. Use TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named App that returns null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the App component. This is the main entry point for your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've created a component named App that returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't defined correctly. Create a functional component named App that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize state for authentication status
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to declare a state variable called isAuthenticated with an initial value of false. Make sure to specify the type as boolean.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The syntax is: const [isAuthenticated, setIsAuthenticated] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have an isAuthenticated state variable initialized to false, ready to track authentication status.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isAuthenticated state variable. This will be essential for tracking whether the user is logged in throughout the OAuth2 PKCE flow.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Used useState, 2) Named the variable isAuthenticated, 3) Set initial value to false, 4) Specified the type as boolean.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just initializing the state. Use useState<boolean>(false) to create an isAuthenticated variable inside your App component.

steps.title: Initialize state for authorization code
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, add another useState hook to initialize a state variable called authorizationCode with an empty string as its initial value.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to provide the type parameter <string> and initialize it with ''.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a second useState hook for a string state
const [authorizationCode, setAuthorizationCode] = useState<string>('');
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: one for authentication status and one for the authorization code.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a state variable to store the authorization code from the OAuth redirect.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with the type parameter <string> and initializing it with an empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to add a useState hook for a string state variable called authorizationCode.

steps.title: Define helper to generate code verifier
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function called generateCodeVerifier that returns a random string. This function will be used later to create a secure code verifier for PKCE.
steps.hint: You can create a function that generates a random string using crypto.getRandomValues and base64url encoding. For now, you can return a placeholder string like 'placeholder-verifier' to establish the function structure.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will now contain a generateCodeVerifier function that returns a string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the generateCodeVerifier function. This will be essential for creating secure PKCE code verifiers.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named exactly 'generateCodeVerifier' and returns a string value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The generateCodeVerifier function isn't properly defined. Check that you've created a function with the correct name that returns a string.

steps.title: Define helper to generate code challenge
steps.instruction: Define a function named generateCodeChallenge that takes a code verifier string as a parameter and returns a string. This function will be used to generate the PKCE code challenge from the verifier. Place it after your existing generateCodeVerifier function.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts a verifier parameter and returns a string. You can start with a simple implementation that returns the verifier directly for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a generateCodeChallenge function that takes a verifier string and returns a string.
successCriteria: The code must include a function named generateCodeChallenge with a string parameter and string return type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the generateCodeChallenge function. This function will be essential for creating the PKCE code challenge from the verifier in the OAuth2 flow.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named exactly 'generateCodeChallenge', takes a string parameter, and returns a string. Check that you've included the proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The generateCodeChallenge function is not properly defined. Make sure you create a function with that exact name that accepts a string parameter and returns a string.

steps.title: Define login handler function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleLogin inside your App component. This function should be async and not take any parameters.
steps.hint: Create an async function that will handle the login flow. Use the function keyword or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async handleLogin function defined inside your App component.
successCriteria: The handleLogin function should be defined as async and placed inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the handleLogin function. This will be the main entry point for the OAuth2 PKCE login flow.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure handleLogin is defined as an async function inside the App component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleLogin function isn't defined correctly. It should be an async function inside the App component.

steps.title: Define token exchange handler
steps.instruction: Define a function named exchangeCodeForToken that takes two parameters: code (string) and verifier (string), and returns a Promise<string> representing the access token.
steps.hint: Create an async function that will eventually make a POST request to exchange the authorization code for an access token. For now, just define the function signature and return a placeholder promise.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named exchangeCodeForToken is defined with the correct TypeScript signature, ready to be implemented in later steps.
successCriteria: The function must be named exchangeCodeForToken, accept two string parameters (code and verifier), return a Promise<string>, and be defined in the global scope of the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've defined the token exchange handler with the correct TypeScript signature. This function will be used to exchange the authorization code for an access token.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named exchangeCodeForToken, takes two string parameters (code and verifier), and returns a Promise<string>. Check that you've used proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition doesn't match the requirements. Please define a function named exchangeCodeForToken that accepts two string parameters and returns a Promise<string>.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: In your App component's return statement, add a main container div with className 'app' that contains an h1 element with the title 'OAuth2 PKCE Flow Demo'.
steps.hint: Start by returning a div with the className 'app', then place an h1 element inside it with the specified text.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns a basic layout structure with a main container and a title heading.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the main container structure with the app title.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your App component returns a div with className 'app' containing an h1 with the exact title 'OAuth2 PKCE Flow Demo'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main container structure isn't quite right. Your App component should return a div with className 'app' that wraps an h1 element containing the title 'OAuth2 PKCE Flow Demo'.

steps.instruction:
Inside your component's return statement, add a paragraph (

The paragraph must contain both state values: isAuthenticated and authorizationCode, displayed within the same

steps.title: Add login button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, add a button with the text 'Login with OAuth2 PKCE' and wire its onClick event to call the handleLogin function.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element inside the container div. Use the onClick prop and pass handleLogin as the handler.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button with the text 'Login with OAuth2 PKCE' appears in the UI, and clicking it triggers the handleLogin function.
successCriteria: The button element must have the text 'Login with OAuth2 PKCE' and an onClick prop set to handleLogin.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the login button and wired it to the handleLogin function. The button will now trigger the OAuth2 PKCE flow when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the button text is exactly 'Login with OAuth2 PKCE' and the onClick prop correctly references handleLogin.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly configured. Ensure you've added a <button> element with the correct text and onClick handler.

steps.title: Add token exchange button
steps.instruction: Add a button with the text 'Exchange Code for Token' that calls the exchangeCodeForToken function when clicked.
steps.hint: Place the button after the existing login button in the JSX. Use the onClick prop to call exchangeCodeForToken with the current authorizationCode state value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button that calls a function with state value
<button onClick={() => handleAction(someState)}>Perform Action</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A new button labeled 'Exchange Code for Token' appears below the login button, which when clicked will trigger the token exchange process.
successCriteria: The button should have the text 'Exchange Code for Token' and an onClick handler that calls exchangeCodeForToken with the authorizationCode state value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the token exchange button. This completes the basic UI for the PKCE flow demonstration.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but it might be missing the correct text or onClick handler. Make sure the button says 'Exchange Code for Token' and calls exchangeCodeForToken with the authorizationCode when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or doesn't match the requirements. Add a button element with the text 'Exchange Code for Token' and wire it to call the exchangeCodeForToken function.
